SIR A. B. WALKER.
We take the following from the "Star " of Thar..

r-gfr Andrew Barclay Walker. the brewer bar- onet. is sail to be the wealthist commoner in England. When a yonng fellow, getting on for half it century ago, he managed a poblie-house at Liverpool belonging to his father, a small brewer. In the days when the public-houses were coining money Sir Andrew added house after house to Isis property until " Walker's Warrington " was seen at almost every corner. Like King siurlse. everything he touched turned to gold. also the owner of mines which bring him in a fabulous income. Sir Andrew is a middle-sized,trim-lookingman.with White moustache and sink whiskers, very listi/ws.' !in appearance ; and though considerably on the : wrong side of sixty Ras married a second time : quite recently, the tulle being Miss Okeover, one lof Iler Majesty's maids of honor. Sir Andrew is the owner of several tine estates and of a beautiful yacht which cost something like VALOUR The Cahona is a stream of luxury. The grand saloon is magnificent. The suite is of oak, upholstered in brown-gold plush; the Broadwood piano, writing desks and cabinets are in carved oak to match. The walls of oak are interspersed with forty or fifty , bronze panels in relief ; and the table cloths, with Oriental embroidery, cost nearly £1551 each. Nearly all the crowned heads of Europe huve been aboard the yacht, the Prince of Wales being a particular friend of its fortunate owner. Turning over the !pages of the visitors book.the present writernoticed the signatures of .llbert Edware, .'slexandra, Albert Victor, George, Louise, Victoria: Marie, Grand Duchesse rio ltoeoie Oscar, King of Sweden, and a host of others. With all hi, wealth,Sir Andrew is no i men. parvenu. Ile compelled his son to go t hrough the" mill" --to learn the ins and ontsof the brewing Moine.., even to the washing out of hairels. Ile has given very large sums away for public pur- poses. Personally he is a quiet and som,lhat retiring man. and extremely courteous. It in :literally true that he does not know Om ex- tent of his own wealth. which runs into millions.

ACCIDENT AT STOCKPORT.
SEVEN PERSONS INJURED.

A serious railway accident, fortunately unattended by loss of life, occurresl at the London and North-Western Station at Stm.kport about live o'clock on Monday evening. The delver of tin. Bristol express, when ap- proaching the station, noticed that the signals were against him, bat owing to Om failure of the brakes he was unable to naluee speed to less than 15 miles an hour. 1 Ache drew near tle down platform he 1110 t a loyal 1 train standing on tho• instals, anti seeing that a colliion was inevitable he gave the alarm signal then succeeds,' • in safely jumping fn,u the engine. A moment later a bond craslbacconsissinied by theslirieksof injunal persons, notified that an accident had happened. The express engine dashisl into the hilld coneh of the teal train, and by the force of the shock lifted it several feet from the rads. The carriage fell. the six-foot, lueltily on its wheels. The occupants of the hind cowl, of the Isseal train and the front carriages of theexpnws were violently . thrown (nail their seats and many Ed them wt., badly shaken and bruised. A large staff of OffiehllA, aided by 1 passengers, at once rushed to their assistance, and the wounded psuih. were yarefully removed to, the waiting- rooms adjoining. Medical men wen. immediately called in, and it WaA found that seven of the passwgers were severely injured. One lady had her face baolly cut and the Miadle linger of OW hand broken. An ingenious arrangement which Mr. Nice. agent on the Latchford section, has erected for the separating and washing of the ballast got from the cutting, previous to its being mined for the concrete walls, is in use at Latch- ford locks. The cutting at Latchford locks is, for com siiterablv more than half its depth, through hard sand- stone, tine sides being perpendicular.
